terms.latin: ācta diurna, āctōrum diurnōrum n. pl.
evidence: Suet. Jul. 20: ut tam senātūs quam populī diurna ācta cōnfierent et pūblicārentur (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The daily record of the senate and the people that Caesar had published (Suet. Jul. 20): the Roman newspaper, read in the provinces and the armies (Tac. A. 16.22). Also diurna alone, or diurna āctōrum scrīptūra (Tac. A. 3.3). A weekly is ācta hebdomadālia (Traupman 351).
Classically a day’s ration, and once a diary (Lewis & Short). A morning paper, diārium mātūtīnum; an evening paper, diārium vespertīnum (Traupman 351).
Classically a day-book or diary (Cic. Quinct. 57, Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: diurna populī Rōmānī per prōvinciās, per exercitūs cūrātius leguntur, ut nōscātur quid Thrasea nōn fēcerit.
phrases.english: The daily gazette of the Roman people is read with special care in the provinces and the armies, to find out what Thrasea has not done.

phrases.latin: cum ex dignitāte populī Rōmānī repertum sit rēs inlūstrīs annālibus, tālia diurnīs urbis āctīs mandāre
phrases.english: since it has been found fitting for the dignity of the Roman people to leave great events to history, and such things to the city’s daily gazette
